title: More Education, Less Employment: India's Graduates Face the Steepest Jobless Rates
excerpt: PLFS data shows unemployment climbing with every level of schooling — about 13% for graduates against a 3.1% national rate — while Azim Premji University puts joblessness near 40% for graduates aged 15-25.
body:
• PLFS data cited by India Today shows unemployment rises with education in India: graduate unemployment is about 13%, while the overall unemployment rate for people aged 15 and above was 3.1% in PLFS 2025.
  • Youth unemployment (ages 15-29) was 9.9% and unemployment among people with secondary education or above was 6.5%, even as 67.8% of people aged 15 and above had completed at least secondary education.
  • Azim Premji University's State of Working India 2026 estimates graduate unemployment near 40% for ages 15-25 and 20% for ages 25-29, with about 5 million graduates added a year between 2004-05 and 2023 against about 2.8 million finding employment.
  • For diaspora families funding a degree in India: only 23.6% of workers were in regular wage or salaried employment in 2025, so judge a course by its placement record and first-job outcomes, not enrolment alone.

India is producing more graduates than at any point in its history, and the official labour data shows a paradox that families across the country — and in the diaspora — are living with: the more education a young Indian has, the more likely they are to be unemployed. India Today's analysis of Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) data frames it as "more education, less employment" — a jobs challenge that sits underneath India's low headline unemployment rate.

The Numbers Behind the Paradox

The PLFS figures for 2025 put the overall unemployment rate for people aged 15 and above at 3.1%. That headline hides the split by education. Unemployment among young people aged 15-29 was 9.9%, and among people with secondary education or above it was 6.5%, according to analysis of the same PLFS data by Policy Circle. Graduate unemployment stands at about 13% — roughly four times the national rate — and a PLFS-based breakdown shows the rate climbing at each step: 0.22% for below-primary schooling, 1.93% at secondary level, 4.38% at higher-secondary, 8.64% for diploma holders and 13.03% for graduates.

https://x.com/OwenGregorian/status/2112683154486227031

The longer-run research is starker for the youngest graduates. The State of Working India 2026 report by Azim Premji University estimates graduate unemployment among 15-25-year-olds at nearly 40%, compared with 20% among those aged 25-29. Between 2004-05 and 2023, roughly five million graduates were added each year while about 2.8 million found employment, and graduates now account for about two-thirds of unemployed youth. Less than 7% of male graduates secure a permanent salaried job within a year of graduating.

"Graduate unemployment has stayed stubbornly high, between 35 and 40 percent, for over four decades. But the scale has grown — India is producing far more graduates in the past few years than jobs for them."

— Rosa Abraham, lead author, State of Working India 2026

Why a Degree No Longer Opens the Door by Itself

The data does not show that education causes unemployment. Workers with less schooling are absorbed quickly into informal and casual work, while graduates wait — often for years — for jobs that match their qualifications. As Dainik Jagran's analysis of the PLFS Annual Report 2025 puts it, more education raises expectations faster than the economy creates suitable jobs. Qualification inflation compounds the problem: a bachelor's degree becomes the minimum, then a master's, then certificates and internships are layered on top.

Job quality is the other half of the story. In 2025, 56.2% of Indian workers were self-employed and 20.2% were casual labour; only 23.6% held regular wage or salaried work, up from 22.4% in 2024. Manufacturing's share of employment rose only slightly, from 11.6% to 12.1%, while agriculture still accounted for 43%. A graduate counted as "employed" may be in a family enterprise, gig work or a job unrelated to their degree — NITI Aayog has separately flagged that only 8.25% of graduates work in roles aligned with their qualifications.

What This Means for Families

For diaspora households paying tuition in India, or for relatives weighing a return, the practical reading is narrow and concrete: a degree still pays when a graduate gets hired — graduate salaries remain substantially higher than non-graduate pay — but the time to the first suitable job is the risk. Courses should be judged on apprenticeship links, placement rates and time-to-first-job, and families should budget for a longer, exam-heavy transition after graduation rather than assuming employment follows the degree automatically.

What to Watch

The policy debate is shifting from counting jobs to measuring their quality — earnings, security and social protection. Training programmes cannot compensate for a shortage of productive firms willing to hire, Policy Circle notes. Whether private-sector job creation in smaller cities and in manufacturing can absorb five million new graduates a year is the question the next PLFS rounds will answer.
